prs.body:
## Description

The nightly System CI installs the tron apt package that `publish-deb.yml` builds with `make deb` from the CMake preset `deb`, and that preset never set `TRON_AMX_DISPATCH`. The three packages built since PR #3879 merged therefore shipped without the AMX attention kernels, and the nightly could not show their effect. This PR adds `"TRON_AMX_DISPATCH": "ON"` to the `deb` preset and updates one paragraph of `README.ci.md`, and the resulting package keeps the AVX path on CPUs without AMX (check 3 below, on the AMD nightly machine).

PR #3879 delivered Attention on Intel AMX feature. Currently the feature is disabled by compile flag `TRON_AMX_DISPATCH`. This PR enables the flag, and brings AMX testing to CI.  



## How to check if binary is built with AMX
- On the installed rinzler, `strings  <path to rinzler> | grep -c -x TRON_AMX_DISABLE`, 1 means AMX is built, 0 not.


## Testing

1. **On delphi-3bda** CI runs with this PR change passed the `strings` test as described above and achieved expected perf boost.
2. **on andoria-b1a3** CI runs with this PR change passed the `strings` test as described above and delivered no regression:

|Model | 9/16 nightly | 9/18 nightly| AMX change|
|---|---|---|---|
|Llama 3.2 3B TP2 @32u | 228.60 | 230.10 | 231.14 |
|Llama 3.1 8B TP2 @8u |149.77 | 150.79 | 150.64 |
|Qwen 3 4B TP2 @8u  | 207.87 | 206.54 | 209.37 |
|Qwen 3 4B TP4 @8u  | 186.55 | 184.47 | 187.35 |
|GPT OSS 120B TP4 @8u | 122.71 | 123.75 |123.73|
prs.title: AMX to CI - CMakePresets: compile the AMX attention kernels into the .deb package

prs.body:
Timed waits update two atomic counters shared by all threads, although only diagnostic tests read them. Those updates add contention during inference. This PR makes them optional with `TRON_MWAIT_STATS`, defaulting to **OFF**. `-DTRON_MWAIT_STATS=ON` restores the counters and their test assertions. The wait mechanisms and timeout logic stay the same.

FPGA CI runs both settings in one CMake build. Diagnostic tests share the existing libraries and add three compiled objects: the instrumented wait implementation and two test sources. Each executable links exactly one wait implementation. Coverage enables counters; inference benchmarks leave them off.

At previous head `57bf6cf3`, the additional diagnostic targets took **4.8 seconds on four Andoria-11 CPU cores**, with compiler caching disabled. That covers three compilations and two links; all 201 existing objects remained unchanged. It measures the added targets, not total CI time.

The original four-card diagnostic removed only counter increments from combined routing/rounding head `7a5b21d4`. GPT-OSS-20B used 2,048 input tokens and 512 output tokens per request:

| Concurrent users | Decode per user, tokens/s, counters on → off | Total output, tokens/s, counters on → off |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 286.31 → 318.53 (+11.25%) | 207.59 → 223.49 (+7.66%) |
| 4 | 183.95 → 196.71 (+6.94%) | 421.10 → 438.54 (+4.14%) |

Decode measures generation after prompt processing; total output includes prompt processing and all users. Values are medians of four process results per setting, with one warmup and three measured iterations. Run order alternated, and all eight paired throughput comparisons improved. These are the retained counter-on/off measurements.

The fresh integrated comparison no longer shows the earlier large four-card slowdown. Median paired total throughput improves by 0.31–1.14% for one user and falls by 0.50–0.94% for four users; reported prompt-completion time increases by 0.70–3.52% across the six configurations. The fresh comparison in [#4367](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4367) uses this counter fix in **both** builds: main `0a51385e` versus #4367 + #4366 on that same main. It tests the numerical changes with counters disabled; it does not remeasure the speedup from disabling counters. [#4374](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/issues/4374) retains the complete results and integration status.

After reconciliation with main `ff0a47e8`, all four wait tests pass on Andoria-11. Compiler, linker and symbol checks confirm the default-OFF and named-ON variants, one wait implementation per executable and four distinct test registrations. `make build-test`, formatting and lint pass. The earlier developer host suite reported 80 passes, one skip and the #4437 failure because its limited catalogue omitted models expected by `t_chat_template`. The current hosted host test passes. Earlier global-ON, coverage, packaging, 72 helper-test and four Slice timing checks remain recorded at `57bf6cf3`; reconciliation preserves that implementation.

Both fresh GPT-OSS comparison builds include the unchanged wait implementation on main `0a51385e`. Their actual production objects and links omit the counters. At head `c03347b1`, [Build Tron](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/35753324469/job/106892474671), [Test host](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/35753324469/job/106892475697), [Test FPGA](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/35753324469/job/106892474054) pass. The earlier cache wait stopped before the C++ build; #4535 tracks that infrastructure problem.
prs.title: Disable wait statistics by default

prs.body:
Reduce software and FPGA attention separately as each becomes ready, then combine the two results. FPGA passes merge while later passes run; each query finishes once both of its reductions are complete. The plan fixes the merge order; regrouping can change rounding relative to main.

**Long context improves both prompt and generation.** Fresh Dice measurements against main `ab13fef7b`:

| Context | Prompt: lower TTFT | Generation: higher tok/s |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 2K | equivalent | **2.17%** |
| 32K | **7.57%** | **15.9%** |
| 88K | **16.2%** | **29.5%** |

GPT-OSS-120B TP4, one user, hardware attention on, 128 generated tokens. Medians of three isolated requests per context/version on the same Genoa/four-FPGA partition.

Eight-user controls (four per TP4 partition, ten isolated iterations per partition):

- **GPT-OSS-120B, 2K prompt / 514 generated tokens, hardware attention on:** TTFT improves **2.07%**; generation is equivalent.
- **Llama 3.1 8B, 1,920 prompt / 130 generated tokens, hardware attention off:** prompt and generation are equivalent.

Changes under 1% are equivalent. The two-stage ordering is equivalent to the previous PR head in these workloads; no regression of 1% or more was measured against main.

Validation: `make build-test`, three focused attention suites covering both readiness orders and DMA lifetime, and refreshed 1/2/4-slice test benchmarks passed. The host suite had **88 passed, 0 skipped, 1 failed**: the unchanged proxy/Dice launch issue tracked in [#4418](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4418).
prs.title: HW attention: start join work earlier (long context win)

Shuffled placement retains bookkeeping it never uses and keeps its random generator alive after construction. Remove the unused `total_tensors` and `placed_tensors` fields, the empty destructor, and the now-unneeded `<atomic>` include.

Make the random generator local to the constructor, where it creates the shuffled tensor-rank list. Its seed, shuffle operation, rank consumption, and placement sequence are unchanged.

prs.body:
Shuffled placement locks its tensor-rank list, but the shared device-mask table and tile cursor remain unsynchronized. Placement runs serially during model loading, so this lock does not establish a supported concurrent operation and obscures the actual contract.

Remove the rank-list mutex and its lock guard. Rank consumption, tile rotation, and seeded shuffle order are unchanged. This cleanup does not add concurrent placement support.
prs.title: Remove partial locking from serial placement

prs.body:
MoE schedule ownership and expert placement currently depend on the generated field that stores a routing. That couples logical router identity to storage and prevents distinct routers from sharing a field. This PR associates schedules and placement coordinates with `MoeRouterId`, and validates schedule use against the router that last populated the field.

## Why field identity is insufficient

A logical router represents one MoE routing operation; its routing field holds the resulting token-to-expert assignment. If two routers eventually share storage, they must retain separate schedules and placement identities.

Illustrative pseudocode for a stale schedule after reuse:

```text
route(router=0, output=shared)  // builds schedule_0
route(router=1, output=shared)  // builds schedule_1
matmul(routing=shared, schedule=schedule_0)
```

Previously, validation rejected the second producer of `shared` outright. Merely allowing repeated field names would leave the schedule check unable to distinguish the two owners: both refer to `shared`. The new checks allow distinct router IDs to populate the same field, but reject the final matmul because its schedule belongs to router 0 while the field contains router 1's routing.

## Carry logical ownership through lowering and emission

Loopy-to-Tron lowering now records router IDs against the original Loopy routing names, independently of the Tron fields those names resolve to. Expert weights retain that logical ID for placement, and `MoeScheduleInfo` records it as the schedule's owner.

C++ emission uses this ownership to select the schedules built by each routing operation and to enumerate that router's expert-weight tensors for placement. When a schedule's C++ type needs the expert count, emission follows its owner ID to the corresponding route statement and routing declaration.

Tron validation requires unique router IDs and walks statements in order, tracking the latest router to write each field. Each expert matmul must use a schedule owned by that router and declared for the same weight tensor.

This builds on routing-name resolution in [#4458](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4458). Lowering still creates one routing field per logical router here; later stack layers analyze reuse, materialize shared fields, and preserve runtime buffer capacity.

## Validation

The changed TronCheck cases accept distinct router IDs sharing a field and reject a schedule from the previous router after that field is refilled. Adapted cases cover matching schedule ownership, rejection of a different weight source, and duplicate router-ID rejection, including at the C++ emission boundary.
prs.title: ingest: Separate MoE router identity from storage

prs.body:
Define the prequant entry header, layout-based validation, cache-root selection, and hashed entry paths in `h/tron/hardware/prequant_cache.hpp`. The caller supplies the source identity, including distinctions between quantization transforms; synthesized tensors are excluded because their seed is absent from that identity.

At this branch boundary the format has no payload digest and does not inspect source bytes. Tests cover header equality, environment controls, and containment of entry paths for hostile source IDs.

Production I/O is deferred: `ishapira/prequant-02-io` uses the header in `prequant_cache_reader::open` in the same header. `ishapira/prequant-04-writer` adds publication through `prequant_cache_writer`. The loader consumes these helpers in `ishapira/prequant-07-load-impl`, in `h/tron/hardware/tensor.hpp::dtensor::try_read_cache_file_into_hbm`.

Local verification (September 16): this branch has a completed baseline-relative PASS at `3cb749240d3539284ea8ebf69b7a2dfe506797d4` in current attempt `N4MJ5g`, on recorded trunk `282955f1b08126f5fcf4bd8382146cfa388ea011`. The raw configured Nix gate fails only the measured inherited `hlint` and `treefmt-check` checks. The complete 57-branch gate finished with baseline-relative PASS (exit 0); this is not a clean Nix pass or a product CI success claim. Required CI is tracked separately at the published head.
prs.title: prequant: Define the cache format and identity key

prs.body:
MoE routing intermediates currently receive separate storage even when an earlier routing is no longer needed before a later one is built. This PR computes which routings can share a storage slot and when to prepare its synchronization channel, providing the plan that the next stack layer uses to share routing fields.

## Planning reusable routing slots

`RoutingAssignment` maps each routing intermediate to the first-written routing that owns its planned slot. The allocator processes routings in first-write order, so ownership follows execution order even when declarations appear in a different order.

For an illustrative example, suppose `routing_a` is written at statement 0 and last read at statement 1, while `routing_b` is written at statement 24. If both have eight experts, select two experts per token (`topK = 2`), and have compatible channel requirements, the plan maps both to `routing_a`. Preparation for `routing_b` is scheduled after `routing_a`'s last read and before `routing_b`'s write executes.

Routings use a separate slot pool within the existing buffer allocator. This reuses its lifetime checks, channel compatibility rules, and reuse-gap heuristic, which leaves separation between uses to limit additional waiting. Matching expert counts and `topK` values ensure that a shared slot can hold either routing. Overlapping lifetimes or incompatible requirements receive separate slots.

## Stack scope

The parent, [#4459](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4459), separates logical router identity from storage identity. This layer returns the routing assignment and applies its preparation schedule, while lowering still creates a distinct field and guard channel for each routing. Scheduled operations retain the original routing names and therefore resolve to those individual channels here. [#4461](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4461) consumes the assignment to materialize shared fields and channels.

## Validation

Analysis tests cover shared ownership independent of declaration order, exactly one preparation between successive routing lifetimes, and separate slots for overlapping lifetimes or mismatched expert counts and `topK` values.
prs.title: ingest: Compute reusable MoE routing assignments

Problem:
Runtime model modules need a frozen discovery and factory ownership contract
before any loader, DSO, or production consumer can use them.

Change:
Add ABI-major-1 query, status/error, scheduler factory, compatibility-token,
and descriptor types. Document exact-build scope, forward-pass performance
boundary, discovery validation, and factory ownership/error rules.

Invariant:
This is an additive, unused header. No runtime behavior, public API, build
target, or consumer changes.

Enables:
Later patches can generate manifests and fingerprints, implement factory shims,
and validate modules against this contract.

Validation:
Standalone C++23 syntax compile passed with GCC; clang-format, Note lint,
diff check, and all pre-commit hooks passed.

prs.body:
Rotating and shuffled placement duplicate the calculation used to fill their cyclic device-mask tables. Extract that calculation into `cyclic_replica_mask` and call it from both table-building loops, preserving the existing placement sequence.

For table entry `i`, the old loops selected device positions `i * replicas` through `i * replicas + replicas - 1`, wrapping through the supplied device set. The helper computes those same positions directly. The tables, cursor preservation, and shuffled starting ranks remain unchanged.

The subsequent [strategy-ownership PR](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4198) reuses this helper to select each tile's devices directly and removes the tables.
prs.title: Extract cyclic replica mask calculation

prs.body:
Parallelize software attention within a page when hardware offload or sliding windows leave too few pages to keep cores busy. Workers process disjoint query ranges in both Ready and Pending phases, preserving each query's full-page reduction and section-completion accounting.

Split only single-page sections with at least 32 relevant queries, when productive page/KV-head tasks number at most half the workers. The planner accounts for worker load, speed, and setup/join overhead; it requires a 10% predicted improvement and chooses the fewest pieces within 3% of the best predicted completion time.

Measured GPT-OSS prompt throughput improves **2.38% at 2K** and **4.28% at 32K**; generation improves **1.03% at 32K**. Llama controls are equivalent to main in both phases. Changes under 1% are reported as equivalent.

| Model | Users / instances | Prompt / gen tokens | Prompt throughput | Gen throughput |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 2,049 / 128 | +2.38% | equivalent |
| GPT-OSS 120B TP4, HW attention on | 1 / 1 | 32,769 / 128 | +4.28% | +1.03% |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP4, handwritten | 8 / 2 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP2, handwritten | 8 / 4 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.2 3B TP2, handwritten | 32 / 4 | 800 shared + 199 / 335 | equivalent | equivalent |
| Llama 3.1 8B TP2, generated | 8 / 4 | 1,920 / 130 | equivalent | equivalent |

Matched runs against main (`282955f1`) used Dice on andoria-cf8c: three isolated requests per context/version for GPT-OSS and at least 20 instance-iteration samples per version for Llama. Prompt counts include BOS where applicable. No throughput loss of 1% or more was measured in these comparisons.

Validation: `t_llama_unit`, `t_ranged_mask`, full build, formatting, and [CI host and FPGA tests](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/actions/runs/35258393447/attempts/2) pass. Tests cover Ready/Pending splits, sliding windows, query coverage, completion accounting, and cases where splitting should be declined.
prs.title: Split software attention pages across cores by query (for small page and large query counts)

prs.body:
Placement strategies currently overwrite a shared table of device masks and its tile cursor. Router and expert overrides must save and restore that cursor to preserve the wrapped strategy's position. Give each strategy ownership of tile selection and remove the global `device_placer` entirely.

## Keep selection state in each strategy

`PlacementStrategy` exposes two operations: `begin_tensor(request)` identifies the logical tensor, and `next_tile_devices()` returns the devices that will store its next tile. Placement processes one tensor at a time; beginning another tensor changes what subsequent tile selections mean.

Rotating and shuffled placement keep their own counters. Router and expert wrappers retain the current tensor's override mode or device mask and delegate both operations only for tensors handled by their base. An override therefore leaves the base strategy's cursor untouched.

For example, ordinary tiles can select devices 0 and 1, an expert override can select device 0, and the next ordinary tile resumes at device 2. The earlier [expert-rotation fix](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4531) establishes this behavior using shared-cursor save/restore; this refactor preserves it through separate ownership.

## Compute cyclic masks directly

The [parent PR](https://github.com/positron-ai/tron/pull/4536) extracts `cyclic_replica_mask` to fill the existing mask tables. This PR calls the same helper directly for each tile: it selects `replicas` consecutive positions starting at `rotation * replicas`, wrapping through the device set. Rotating placement retains its counter across tensors. Shuffled placement starts each tensor at the next rank from its existing seeded shuffle, then advances once per tile. This preserves the selection sequence without constructing or copying mask tables, making `device_placer` unnecessary.

## Preserve the loading boundary

`place_on_devices()` becomes a function with the same call syntax. It asks the installed strategy for the next tile's mask, intersects it with available devices, rejects an empty result, and records placement for logging. Standalone allocations still use the current device mask when no strategy is installed.

The strategy remains globally installed, and loaders still use `with_placement`. The method rename, unused shuffled-state cleanup, mutex removal, and cyclic-mask helper extraction precede this PR; the subsequent placement-context PR changes the owning scope and caller interface.
prs.title: Give placement strategies ownership of tile selection
